utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Defence seem to be all here. Prosecution, Mr. Thayer, Mr. McCloskey, and all the accused are here. All right. So before we bring in the witness, please, there are a couple of things. You will recall some time back we were dealing with a Prosecution motion for protective measures relating to two witnesses in particular, Witness number 70 and Witness number 80. This was filed on the 4th of December after an invitation by ourselves. Basically, in its motion the Prosecution requested the continuance in force of the protective measures which had been granted in Krstic. Going through the records of file before proceeding for our Christmas and New Year's recess, we noted that although we have already ruled orally as regards Witness number 70, we haven't finalised the protective measures process relating to Witness number 80. In Krstic, this individual was granted pseudonym and both voice and facial distortion. Our proposal to you is, if you can try and refresh your memory on this, our proposal is that we try and rule orally on this before we go into recess, and I would appreciate if I have a joint response from the Defence teams. The other thing is perhaps more important, although the first one is also important, of course, but what I'm going to say now, please, is take it as guidance on something that we believe is of imperative, of paramount importance. Now, we have these last weeks been dealing with testimony relating or concerning intercepts. The Defence teams have at different stages of these proceedings, even basically before we started the trial proper, intimated that they had serious concerns and serious objections relating to practically all intercepts that the Prosecution meant to introduce in -- in evidence in this case. We also intimated to you that more or less although many of the decisions that we will take on admissibility issues will be reserved to the final stages of the trial when we are deliberating. Intercepts is not one of them. Intercepts is a matter that we would like to deal with and decide upon during the trial, during the trial, so that you are all in a position to know where we stand and where you stand in relation to these documents. So we've been more or less thinking about how best to proceed. We haven't concluded the testimony on intercepts, on intercepts, but we have gone far enough to enable us to give you guidance. So our intention is to rule on these intercepts and their admissibility when all the evidence on them has been led by the Prosecution. That's when we intend to rule on the admissibility. In other words, it would give you -- this would give you the opportunity of knowing what the case of the Prosecution is relating to these intercepts, and then you should be in a position to make your submissions on the admissibility aspects of these -- of these documents or on these pieces of evidence. So our intention is to alert you already that more or less at that stage we'll be requesting you to provide us, the Trial Chamber, with written submissions and listing and explaining your arguments and objections regarding each intercepts. You will, of course, make submissions of a general nature but also of a specific nature. And of course the Prosecution will be given adequate time and opportunity to -- to respond. This is what we basically wanted to alert you to, giving you prior notice that will be as soon as we have an indication that the Prosecution hasn't got any further substantive material evidence to lead in relation to these intercepts, then we are going to call on you and give you adequate time to file these objections or arguments and submissions. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't wish to complicate the issue, but as you may imagine that once the intercept operators are over, and I guess that's what you're talking about, there will be voluminous evidence from people that are involved in conversations, documents that correspond to the conversations, all that material which will probably go to the end of the case, but I understand that that's not what you're talking about, and -- but that is all part of the intercept package, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. That is fully understandable, and that's exactly not what we had in mind. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that this could be applied not only once we're done with all intercept operators but also when we examine the expert -- or, rather, not the expert but the investigator who worked on intercepts, which is Mrs. Stefanie Frease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic. I think that's a very good idea Mr. Zivanovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I actually wanted to make a submission, and quite frankly the point was on the intercepts, and it's our position that we not only suspect but we reasonably believe that these intercepts were either recreated or created at a time between the period from 1995 when they allegedly made those entries through 1998. There's absolutely no evidence whatsoever to establish this chain of custody that is required for these intercepts. We've seen from, I think, almost every witness and perhaps I'm exaggerating, but I think it's every witness, quite candidly, that there are numerous -- no, no, but I'm making a submission, that there are numerous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will require the submission at the right time. We don't need it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm making a submission right now, Your Honour. Before -- I think it's premature to even suggest to rule on evidence after it is concluded until this Court orders an independent expert to review these books, especially book number 22. I'm asking for an independent review not in a review from the OTP's experts, and I'm asking that because our funds are actually, quite frankly, restrained and we don't have that much money. So I think this Court can respectfully under its guidelines proprio motu order an expert from Holland or preferably someone from Italy where these books were generated from to examine both the paper, the document quality, as well as the ink imprintations as well as the handwriting samples. Those three things one expert can do within a given 30- to 45-day period, I would suggest. I'm asking this Court, given what the Court said and given what the testimony is, that it orders that these documents be seized and either turned over to the Defence so that our expert can make that analysis on these documents, or that the Court takes it upon themselves and give to an independent expert, preferably in Italy. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't expect us to comment on that today, Mr. Ostojic. If we are seized with an ad hoc motion on -- on the matter, of course you will hear what we have to say and when we think we ought to say it. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning all. I just wanted to alert the Court to our tentative schedule with respect to the remaining intercept operators, just maybe to give everybody an idea of the approximate time frame. We have approximately, I believe, 15 intercept operators left, assuming that the Court admits the testimony of some of these intercept operators we've identified pursuant to the Chamber's 92 bis decision. I think we've scheduled them basically through the end of January. Given the way even an optimistic estimate things have been going, that will probably take us through sometime in February. That would also include the testimony of Ms. Frease to whom my learned colleague just referred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I imagine so. I took that for granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So that's just the approximate time period, and that's a pretty optimistic estimate, I'm afraid. That's basically one day. Although these are going to be pure intercept operators. There's going to be one supervisor from -- from MUP that we intend to call. Some of the intercept operators have more intercepts than others, but that's our general estimate right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer, but I think -- let me make it clear. The message is twofold. One is for the Defence to know that we would be expecting you to come forward with your objections. After that you have had an opportunity to know what the Prosecution evidence in regard to intercepts is. The second is that since we are giving this indication to the Defence teams, you have a responsibility to group together the witnesses on intercepts and conclude that phase of the trial as early as possible so that, in other words, you don't fragment the evidence leaving some important like Ms. Frease's testimony to a later stage which would frustrate the whole purpose of the exercise. I think we have said enough on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More than enough I've been told. Thank you. So I think we can bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, yesterday we spoke about how you determined who the participants were in the conversation at tab 1 who were supposedly Mr. Beara and Mr. Krstic. Since your testimony in the Blagojevic case is being offered as evidence, sir, I wish to read the portion of that testimony and to have you just explain that answer to me. And it begins for Your Honours and my learned friends is on page 4141, lines 1 through 17, I believe. Sir, in that testimony they asked you how you determined that they, Colonel Ljubo Beara and General Krstic were the participants in the conversation, and I'd ask that you please listen carefully to your answer on line 4, which states as follows: "Well, first of all, we would always recognise Krstic's voice because he spoke on a number of different occasions. You soon became familiar with his voice because he had a very powerful, resonant voice. We always recognised Krstic. If sometimes we didn't catch the introductory part of the conversation where they would introduce themselves, they would sooner or later in the course of the conversation say their names. If there was no way for us to know who the speakers were, we would just put two question marks, speaker A question mark, speaker B question mark. But if you look at the text of the message, the way they speak to one another, they keep using their names. So it was easy for us to understand who the participants were. This was the channel or, rather, the frequency that he very often spoke on. It was his phone. There were several ways for us to ascertain this." Sir, I'd like you to look and if we can put on the e-court or if we can have the tab, I'm not sure where the book was that the witness had yesterday with the various intercepts, if he could take a look at that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine he still has it or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not before him, Your Honours, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if we could make it available, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And he may not need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, given your answer in Blagojevic on the 7th of November, 2003, can you point out to us where Mr. Beara's name was mentioned and how was it determined that you found that it was Mr. Beara in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: While he's looking, Your Honour, if I can just ask, for purposes of a speedy conclusion to this, if we could have the original logbook with the witness and we'll be looking at that on e-court next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think it's the Prosecution that has to help us there. Madam Usher will oblige.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at my transcript, the happened written portion, there most likely was an introductory part in this conversation which I did not transcribe. Normally the person from the switchboard operator -- switchboard would make the connection between the participants. Typically the one making the call, say, General Krstic, would say, "Would you please get Beara for me, get Ljubo Beara for me."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that. I just want to ask you, do you have an independent recollection of this conversation or are you just speculating as to what may or may not have happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not speculating. Based on my experience, based on how I did this, I'm telling you how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So your --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us, sir, you remember the conversation as you sit here today; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation is familiar, as is my handwriting. But as for the response that you're looking for, namely how I recognised that it was Ljubo Beara, I'm just simply telling you on what basis I was able to recognise. I'm sure that on the switchboard his name was mentioned, and then in the following portions of the conversation Krstic mentions Ljubo, talks to him. His name, Ljubo, is mentioned. As for Ljubo's voice, we had listened to it not only in this dispatch but many times before that. The conversations frequently in which he participated were not relevant, so we would not transcribe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, can you tell me why in November of 2003 you didn't simply answer that when the Prosecutor asked you the question and answer that I just read to you moments ago? You only mentioned that you recognised Krstic's voice, that you felt his voice was rather characteristically unique, and then you go on to proceed that in the course of the conversation they say their names. And I submit to you, sir, that nowhere in the course of the conversation does Mr. Beara say his name, and nowhere in the course of the conversation does General Krstic refer to the gentleman he's speaking to as Mr. Beara. Do you see that? And explain to us why you didn't say that to the Court while you were under oath in November of 2003.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because the question was not formulated as you formulated it now. Otherwise, I would have given a different answer. For example, in one of lines it says, "Ljubo, this is not a secure line." So we know that this was Ljubo. We knew his voice. We knew that there was an introductory portion when the switchboard made the call. We knew that Krstic had to make the call, otherwise how would he get Ljubo on the other side? So I simply didn't write "Ljubo" down, but as soon as I heard who was calling whom, I put the names of participants above the conversation. I simply wasn't interested in anything after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say, sir, that if you were asked a question how did you determine that they were the participants in the conversation, you would have answered it the way you did today; correct? Like you just did. Is that what you're telling us? That the question was improper and had they only asked the question of how did you determine that they were the participants in the conversation, then you would have obviously told them about the introductory material, the recognition of Mr. Beara's voice, et cetera. Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that was answered at line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His answer before, or also last answer was probably because they didn't ask me the question the way you asked. So otherwise I would have told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm asking if that's the question that would have -- no, but there's a reason -- wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's been repeating that there were two fundamental matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That he and they were familiar with the voices. And secondly, that there was an introductory part. So I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I would like just the Court to focus on, and I'll move on, is if the Court looks specifically at the question on page 4141, on line 2 and 3, which is the very question that this witness seems to suggest that he would have answered it if he was asked that question and in fact he was asked that question. But in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this, clarify this for me: You remember the conversation and the meeting you had with Stefanie Frease in November 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Here is what Ms. Frease says in her information report after meeting with you relating specifically to that conversation on page 2, second to the last paragraph. She will states: "He," meaning you, sir, "read the conversation but did not recall it." Is she wrong, sir? Isn't that what you told her, that you don't recall the conversation at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered your question as to whether I remember the conversation, referring to the conversation with Ms. Frease. I remember that. I remember that she showed me this conversation. Now, as to whether I remember this particular conversation, the year when it took place, I most likely was not able to remember it and most likely that's how I answered. I remember Ms. Frease showing this conversation to me. I remember that. Now, as for the particular conversation which took place back then, it would be hard for me to remember it. It would be very hard. Even back then it was already six years after the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, what are the characteristics of Mr. Beara's voice that you recall, if any?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the third time --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, fair enough. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the question is being asked and he --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn to the logbook that's next to you specifically with the ERN number with the last four 4528. Do you see that next to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you see -- thank you. See the handwriting that's on the page that starts at approximately 1450, I think, from the copy? Do you see that handwritten entry of a captured conversation? Yes, right there. Do you see that? It's right there in front --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, I want to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no. Don't turn the page. It's on that page. On the right side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Left or right? Yes, I do remember it. I see it. Yes, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Okay. Maybe I'll finish the question, and we'll --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, it's my fault, thank you. Sir, is the conversation that's reflected on this page and on the next page a conversation that you captured and recorded, meaning wrote down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, who wrote the date 11.7.1995 before above the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my handwriting. I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... solve this for us, sir. Given your testimony both in Blagojevic and here yesterday, I thought you don't usually write dates of conversations, and then you explained to us that you allegedly wrote the date of the conversation on the 16th of July, 1995. Sir, just tell me, do you write dates of a conversation before you actually record or capture the conversation? Do you do it after, or do you do it during the conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we've gone over this ground sufficiently whether or not he writes the date of the conversation every time he transcribes an intercepted conversation or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If -- Your Honour, if I can just reply briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We never covered the 11th of July, 1995, and I think it's -- and that's the only comment I need to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that is a completely different matter. You've covered the other two matters, namely you've asked questions to the witness in relation to writing dates, whether there was a specific instruction and he's explained that. So that has been covered. He has explained that there were times when he wrote it at the end of his shift. And you have also covered the issue of when the transcript was effected, whether it was effected during the -- the listening process or whether it was done after, and that again has been covered by the witness, explaining that when it was something short they would do it. Otherwise, they would leave it. Now you are moving, adjusting your question or the relevance of your question to the issue of the 11th, the events of the 11th of July. If you're restricted to that, yes, go ahead, but please don't try to cover again the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you were with the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tell us what?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I told you you cannot maintain the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I didn't understand that. Okay, I'll ask another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will polish my English. What can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Speakers overlapping] -- perhaps didn't get the proper translation, Your Honour, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, how is it on the 11th of July, 1995 you put the date at the beginning of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said usually. Sometimes I would write it down and sometimes I wouldn't. If I didn't write it in, I knew that it would be put in when it was being entered into the computer. I -- if I did put it in, then it was good, otherwise, I knew that it would be put in later. There was no strict rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to turn to the next five pages or so to ERN number with the last four digits 4535, and that's the intercept that is at tab 1 of your book, sir, that you already have in front of you. Yesterday we were already starting to cover the first four entries of this intercept. And, sir, is it fair to say with respect to the name Sladojevic it is incorrectly placed in that first section of the intercept? Is that your position, that it was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, also the name, the other name that you use, Tasic, that you entered on the fourth line of this first part of this conversation, that was also a mistake; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, am I correct that you form the basis of this opinion after the Krstic trial but before the Blagojevic trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to that conclusion probably when we were trying to enter this intercept onto the computer, because then we were working much more precisely, and then if we needed sometimes we would call for help to be able to transcribe everything. So as for the computer typed intercepts, we were trying to be as precise there as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: Given on these first four lines or first quarter, as I call it, of this intercept, given that you made two mistakes, two errors in names, sir, why didn't you go back to the logbook and simply correct the name? It's in pencil. You could have either scratched it out or wrote over it, could you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Had I known I would be re-reading it, I would have done that. I tried to do it properly on the computer entry. These were notes, notes. Sometimes we used papers, and the notebook was used to jot down notes. But when we were typing it into the computer, then we would really did our best to do it properly, because that was the text that was sent to the centre. The handwritten ones did not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, as you sit here today whether or not you had to call for help or assistance to have this intercept transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know at this point, but if I couldn't transcribe something myself, I always welcomed help. Perhaps somebody could hear better, was at that point better, inclined to pick up whatever that was. As for this intercept specifically, I really don't remember whether I did that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next four lines if you will, sir, where it starts with the initial B on a colon. And the first line says, "But I don't have any here." Do you see that? What doesn't he have --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- in here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read the whole dispatch to see what isn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like this right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you've had 15 or so days ago when you met for five days with Mr. Thayer, I presume you read the entire dispatch; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that was 15 days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understand the question well, it sounds like my learned colleague is asking the witness to get into the mind of the callers in terms of what Colonel Beara is saying he doesn't have any of. Now, if the question is specifically based on what he wrote down, if there's some linguistic or if there's some other reason tied to his actual transcription, I think that's a fair question, but the way it's asked it sounds like he's asking for speculation based on the state of mind of Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also based on what we have heard before that he doesn't remember this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He recognises, he recognises what is written there, but I think he's said on more than one occasion that don't ask him details on the conversation itself because he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think, with all due respect, Your Honour, if every witness comes here and simply says I don't recall details, then they won't look at any document and simply just tell the Court I can't testify to it, I don't recall details. If he really wrote this conversation, this is an opportunity that we can refresh his recollection on the document and he can tell us whether or not he knows. I don't understand the objection by my learned friend. It is quite frankly inappropriate to suggest that there's merely linguistical problems with it, and it's inappropriate for him to conclude as he did as to who the purported participant of the conversation is. But I'll proceed and I'm ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the first four lines do you see where it says, "But I need 30 men." Do you see that? Next time the B, the initial B starts to speak he says, "But I don't have any here." Do you see that? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty people. Then the next one is take from Tasic or Sladojevic. I can't pull up anything from here. Then the next line is, "I don't have any here. I need them tonight, and I will -- today, and I will return them this evening." "Krle, please understand. I cannot explain." So Beara is asking for 30 people from Krstic. I don't know if I'm right, but that's what I conclude on the basis of what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your direct examination with Mr. Thayer after you met with him for five or so days that you knew Mr. Beara or he was a well-known figure; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was known to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us, sir, at that time what you knew Mr. Beara's position to be and/or his duties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I don't remember that, what he was, who he was. What was important to me was to note down his conversations, but as for the rest, there was a service there whose job it was to analyse all of that. We were just taking down the intercept, helping each other to get it down correctly. But the proper technical analysis was conducted at the place where it was supposed to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that was where, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the place where we were sending the computer typewritten dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in the second -- again we're looking at the second four entries. The initial B, supposedly Mr. Beara, says, "I need 15 to 30 men with Boban, Indjic. I can't do anything." Do you see that? Do you see that? What --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What can't he do, sir; do you know? What --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What can't he do; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, the question shouldn't be that. What you should be asking him -- how can he answer for what allegedly the other -- the person --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Speakers overlapping] --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Prosecutor wants to bring a witness to suggest that Mr. Beara was well known but he doesn't know how he's well known but he understood his voice but can't recall what the characteristics are, quite frankly maybe this witness somehow, Your Honour, can speculate to the fact that he would know what was meant when Mr. Beara said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then make your submissions later when the witness is not here and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- when you come to submission stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I have a right to put the case to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are perfectly right, but Mr. Ostojic should learn to let me finish what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was my fault. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ostojic, you can -- the witness has already told you that his job was to transcribe what he heard. His job is not to explain to you what he thinks if he thinks the interlocutors taking part in the conversation had in mind when they were -- how can he explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I move on, Your Honour. I respectfully disagree with the Court but I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the next four lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, if I can interrupt you a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Witness PW-133, just now, just a little time ago, you said that you don't remember what Mr. Beara was or who he was at the time, but you are saying still you remember that you were able to recognise his voice. I have some difficulty understanding that. How can you remember that you recognise at the time Mr. Beara's voice while you don't remember who he was or what he was? Could you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have been a ham radio operator since I was 17, and I've spent thousands and thousands of hours with headphones on and with the equipment. So I was in a situation when I was on a frequency and I heard a conversation, I would know who it was because I had heard them before. I would be able to recognise who the people were who were speaking without having to have them introduce themselves. As a ham radio operator, I had trained my sense of hearing so much to be able to recognise the modulation of people, many people, not just Beara. At that time when I was listening to somebody frequently, the modulation would remain in my head. I can't recall how long it would stay. Right not perhaps I cannot recall, but at that time I was 100 per cent familiar with that voice and I knew it and recognised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, was it your submission that Mr. Beara appears only this note as one of the participants in the intercepted conversation? Is it true? Only in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In total how many?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe in total there's two, I think, where he's a participant, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two or three, and then there's a total of, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm overlapping. And how many notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think over two notebooks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two notebooks in total of how many notebooks do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two hundred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it to be true, Mr. Witness, there are two intercepts, two intercepted conversations among more than 200 notebooks. Then I think you answered in some way -- in one way or another, but I'd like to hear your explanation again. There's only two conversations which were intercepted. Then one may think that you are saying that -- you are saying that you were able to recognise Mr. Beara's voice. Maybe -- yes, one may find it difficult to follow what you're saying, that you were able to recognise Mr. Beara's voice. So if you could explain it to me again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try. Those two intercepts of Mr. Beara were written down. I agree with that. But there are many, many conversations of his that were not written down. They were simply not that important. Maybe it was his conversation with his ex-wife or something, we had a lot of conversations like that, or with his children, or private conversations. Another thing, that tape, if I listened to it before and if it was difficult to transcribe it, I would have to listen to the tape five or six times. So then hopefully after having listened to it so many times I would manage to recall his voice and his modulation. I didn't hear him only one single time and that was it. I was able to hear him from the tape many times. And also, I heard him many times in unimportant conversations. As a ham radio operator, I was trained and I had the ability to recognise modulations. That was very important to us in -- in amateur radio world. Perhaps I had the natural gift for such a thing. But at that time I was able to recognise and remember his modulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And after having read these intercepts and having gone through all the notebooks, you still don't remember who Mr. Beara was and what Mr. Beara was at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still don't recall who Mr. Beara was. Every time I go back home from here I would try not to remember anything. I just had to struggle to make a living. All of these things are something that I really do not want to remember that much. It's still something that was hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry for interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll speed it up, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you can see since you reviewed this intercept several times with my learned friend, on no less than five occasions does the participant who you identify as Mr. Beara state that he either doesn't know what to do, he doesn't have anything here, and he can't do anything. Sir, given that, do you think, having recognised Mr. Beara's voice and purportedly knowing what he was at that time, does that sound like a person who was helpless?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this he cannot sound like a helpless person. He sounds like a person who is missing people, who has a shortage of people, but it does not sound like a helpless person. He cannot sound like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: In the conversation on the third -- or in the middle of the paragraph where you have the initial B. It says, "But I don't have any. If I did, I still wouldn't be asking for the third day." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me give you a hypothetical, sir. If you were supposed to testify yesterday on the 13th of December, and if I made the comment, "I've been waiting for the third day," that would mean that it's the 14th, 15th, and 16th; correct? If I make that statement, I would have made it on the 16th. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you to say that if you're waiting for something for the third day, what you were waiting for was three days ago. You asked for it for the first time three days ago. That's what I understood. But then when you went on, I'm sorry, I didn't get what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I was waiting for it and it was supposed to arrive on the 13th, and if I've waited three days, that means that it should be the 16th of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this exercise is irrelevant to this witness's purpose for being here. You know, we can play different ways of counting days depending on what day you start, and that doesn't help with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I am anticipating Mr. Ostojic's next question. Do proceed, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. From this sentence all I can conclude is that he has already been waiting for three days for something that he asked for three days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's assume that it's the 13th of any given month, okay? And if Mr. Beara --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- were the participant in this conversation says, "They were supposed to arrive on the 13th but didn't," and then he continues to say, "I wouldn't still be asking for the third day." Isn't it correct, sir, that that means that this conversation occurred on the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's debatable. I don't know what day you are calculating from, from the day he's talking, or you start counting three days from the next day. If it's from the day that he's talking, it could be the 13th, 14th and 15th. If you're talking about the next day and another three days, I mean, I really didn't understand which day you were calculating from. If you're counting from the following day after the 13th, then that would be the 16th. But if you're counting on the same day, then -- I don't know. This is my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't have an understanding of it, because in your testimony you say that this conversation could have been captured on the 14th or 15th, and I'm suggesting to you, sir, that it's rather plain, based on what you wrote down, as well as given that you purportedly made the entry of 16 July 1995 that this conversation did not happen on the 14th of July, it did not happen on the 15th of July, but in fact, it happened, if at all, on the 16th of July, 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And he's been asked that question repeatedly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may just respond. An objection can be made if it's asked and answered, but I don't think we covered this ground at all. I don't think we covered this ground at all with specifically this intercept. And he led evidence that was, quite frankly, unfair and irresponsible to lead to suggest that it's the 14th or the 15th. We're going through the intercept right now. This was never asked. It was never asked and, quite frankly, it was never answered. He doesn't like the answer, but he still should try to restrain himself and refrain from objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's calm it down. Basically I think Mr. Ostojic's question is to try and elicit from the witness a revised assessment of when this particular transcript could have been taking place. He is suggesting after having put previous questions that it is more probable than not that it was on the 16th of July that it was transcribed. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And, again, I just believe that that question was asked yesterday in the context of the date he had written down. There was a series of questions that went directly to the date that Mr. Ostojic tried to put to the witness. He believed that the conversation was written down and the answer was clear yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it's unfair that he would suggest to the witness how he should count the days, but we can address that in a later submission, Your Honour, on the [indiscernible] particularly of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the witness needs any lessons on how to count dates. I think he was very clever in answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a question, if you can look on the front page of your document where is says under K: and if you scroll down from the bottom, nine lines from the bottom. It says, "I can't guarantee anything," and this is purportedly by Mr. Krstic, "I can't guarantee anything. I'll take steps." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you explain to us why that supposedly "I'll take steps" was not transcribed in the typewritten form?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it here, "I'll take steps." Under this sentence, "I can't guarantee anything, I'll take steps." Underneath that it says, "Krle, I don't know what to do anymore." Now, your question was something else, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It was exactly that. Where it states, "I can't guarantee anything," and then it's added, "I'll take steps." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right behind the comma, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is, why isn't that phrase or that sentence typed out in the daily report that was issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right now I can't remember that. I can only speculate and I do not wish to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I want to look at the last section here that talks about the 3.500 parcels. Do you see that? Sir, it's my --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- submission that at the time there were 300 or so men in Potocari that were supposedly going to be sent to Bratunac and that in fact if anything was said in this conversation that there was a pause and it was suggested and should have been written with an interval between the 3 and the 5. So the participant that you heard actually said, "3 -- 500," as opposed to 3.500. Am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this 3, 500, to be fully certain I would have to listen to the tape again. But at that point in time I heard 3.500 and that's what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you wrote it down, sir. The typist who typed your conversation after having listened to it purportedly with you, they have a space between the number 3 and the number 5. Do you know why they have a space between the number 3 and the number 5? And I submit that nowhere in any notebook whenever they mention any numbers is there such a space or interval. Do you see that on the typed version, sir? You might have to flip a page or two.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I need to find the typewritten version, because I just have the handwritten version in front of me now. Yes, I see the pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know you weren't the typist, sir, but do you know why there was a pause? And can you just identify what exhibit -- or put it on the ELMO, if I can ask him that, Your Honour, to see which one he's actually looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because there are two of them, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you just point that out for us and point out where you see this pause?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, would if be possible to -- or I don't know that we can. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then if you look at the page prior to that, sir -- well, I think it's the page after that. Mine is in a different order. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher. We have to keep scrolling to find the other typed intercept. I'm not sure what order the Prosecutor has given it to him in, but it's ... Now -- well, that's okay. We can proceed anyway, if the Court allows. It's not there. Okay. Good enough. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we know that the tape doesn't exist, and I appreciate your comment that in order to be sure that we could determine it, would you agree with me, sir, that an intercept operator such as yourself with the experience that you suggest that you have, that, sir, it would have been more appropriate and disciplined when people are discussing numbers to actually write them out instead of writing them numerically? Would that be fair? And the reason that you would write it out instead of write it numerically is because of specificity and clarity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But he answered already.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It was a compound question. That was my only objection, so we just know which part he's answering to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't heard the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers overlapped; the interpreters weren't able to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's divide the question and then -- because Mr. Thayer I think is right, that there is more than one. So it was put to you, sir, that the tape doesn't exist relating to this, and then you were asked whether an intercept operator such as yourself, an experienced intercept operator such as yourself, whether it would have been more proper, more appropriate and orderly, when people are discussing members -- numbers to actually write them down instead of writing them numerically. Writing words in other -- or instead of just numbers. That's the first question that I would like you to answer. To avoid confusion, wouldn't it have been more appropriate if you had written "three thousand," words, rather than numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree. Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then would that be fair. And then the reason he would write it out because of specificity and clarity which I don't think you need to pursue because he's agreeing with you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, why -- why do you agree with Mr. Ostojic, that it would have been more appropriate had you written down the numbers in words rather than numerically only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be more proper, because even when writing out cheques or doing something with your bank account you have to spell the figure out. And, yes, it would have been more proper because now we have a situation because there is a space missing to indicate hundreds and thousands. In my elementary school, I normally put a full stop to indicate thousands, and most likely I told him 3.500 and the typist put in a space, an interval between. And I have it in one version 3.500. So this must be 3.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir. Let me ask you this: If you look at that logbook, and if you look on the opposite page, don't you see a period or a marking that was actually bled through, which is why we think we need an expert but that's not your concern, that that marking was actually bled through and is in exactly that point after the 3? So I'm asking you, sir, to flip the page from one side to the other and you'll see that there's a mark on the opposite page that seems to have been enhanced.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't know which portion you're referring to now. Is it the handwritten one or -- would you please show me this specific place?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will with the assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you put the real notebook on the ELMO so we can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, 4537, the first five lines of it, please, in particular. If you or the technicians could zoom in on that section, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we're looking specifically at the 3 and the 500. Do you see that, sir? Do you see that? Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- I count how many lines or boxes on the grid, and I think if I'm right if you count from the right to the left there are nine such boxes to that period, and what I'm asking you to do, sir, is just kind of hold your finger there and then flip the page backwards, okay, flip the page over, and you'll see right at the point is where there seems to be a mark that was enhanced by you which bled through the paper as we've seen and as you've testified can happen, and that that's actually a -- if we can move it over to the left a little so we can see it on the screen. There we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. The page that we had. Can you bring it down, please? No, that's -- okay. It's my mistake. Yes. And could someone please zoom us in on the third line. Is it the third line?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show me the exact spot?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Court just did, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think for our better understanding, to be able follow your point better and his answer, once he's finished we'd like to see the notebook here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you look on -- oh, sorry. If you look on the screen, maybe he can then find it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to see the notebook. If you could bring it over, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we will not comment, but we have been able to have a good look at it. I suppose if the witness wishes to answer that question or can answer that question he will proceed to answer it and then you move on to your next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you see that dot --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the dot, sir, that you have after the letter 3 in this conversation? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Can I put it up to the light? Can I take it in my hands and lift it up to the light?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I don't see anything on the opposite page -- on the opposite side, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I know we don't have the tape and I know what the typist wrote down, 3 with a space, interval or pause as we've identified it, and then 500. Do you have any independent recollection, sir, as you sit here as to whether or not the participant in this conversation said 3, 500, or if the participant actually said 3.500?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I wrote down 3.500, that means that I heard it. I believe that I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I wrote it down and gave it to somebody else to type it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, as you sit here today, do you have an independent recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time after so much time has gone by, I don't remember. I know that I did that, but right now I cannot remember the exact steps that I took. It's been too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One last point if we can open the book and turn to page 4536, sir. I always seem to have problems with the last part of sentences, but in this one, sir, if you can see where it talks about the Red Berets. Do you see that? It's five lines down. It's on the right-hand side if you can just adjust it. It's five lines down from the top, so we need the top. Then we need it moved over a little. Do you see that, the word "Red Berets"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, was that written at the same time as your other conversation that was captured on this, or was this added later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe and I think that it was at the same time, when the conversation was transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you write everything else, it seems to be, in a hand -- your handwriting there is not printed, but the words "Red Berets" are printed. Can you reconcile how it is that the conversation is primarily handwritten but the word "Red Berets" is printed? Just so we have an understanding of your style.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not just on this page. For example, we have on the other page that "Draga" was written down in capitals. So I did have a habit of emphasising some names. Because I have a rather bad handwriting, I would try to write it clearly. And if there was a name, if there was a location indicated or a frequency, my idea was to highlight it in some way and to ensure that it was written down as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, read the sentence to us that you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, read the sentence to us that precedes this "Red Beret," if you will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Check with Blagojevic, take his Red Berets."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now linguistically if you look at this and if you were -- can you pause or stop after you say "uzmi njeguve." [phoen] Would the sentence still make sense, sir? "Check with Blagojevic, take his."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because take his what?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, they're talking about men throughout the conversation, are they not? But I'm asking you in the B/C/S language that it's proper grammatically where you could have a pause after "uzmi njeguve" period, and that the words "Red Berets" was simply added after the fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was without Red Berets, take his, could perhaps mean take his men, regardless of what men he had. As for Red Berets, it's a notion that doesn't figure here very frequently. So I don't know what that means Red Berets was said here. Had he written men, I would have -- had he said men, I would have written down men. I would not have given it a thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that your unit in the southern site started maintaining and keeping these logbooks; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can help try to jog your memory. You came to the southern site in the spring of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At that time in -- I think you said April or March, in that time, sir, were logbooks such as this kept in the southern site and were you required to keep track of captured conversations in the spring of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. One moment. Stop, stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, just to make the record clear, if it's a compound question I just want to break them up ahead of time so we don't have to go back and do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You know, they argue, Your Honour, about the waste of time and -- but I think -- the interruptions by Mr. Thayer in the last several weeks I think just reflects that the Defence is not wasting their time. We did ask yesterday if we can ask compound questions. The Prosecution constantly asks leading questions and compound questions. Respectfully we do not object. We do not smirk either. However, Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. Stop. It's a good thing that we will be going in recess. I think it's a compound question and both questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And both questions -- please don't interrupt me, Mr. Ostojic. And both questions have been put already more than once yesterday, both by the Prosecution and by yourself. One is whether logbooks such as this one were kept in the southern site in the spring of April, that's March, April of 1995, and that was answered yesterday. And whether he was required to keep track of captured conversations in the spring of 1995. Perhaps that even needs clarification. What do you mean by keeping track of captured conversations? Whether to -- in other words, to transcribe them in a notebook. If that is what you mean, yes, that has been answered. If you mean something different, then it hasn't been answered. But the rest has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm merely trying to refresh the recollection of this witness by jogging his memory with the time that he came to this site, which was in the spring of 1995, and I don't think it's been put to him whether or not at the spring of 1995, whether it was April or March, whether these logbooks were in existence and whether they were required at that time to make entries such as those that we see in July and August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, did you already give us this information yesterday? You confirmed yesterday that more or less in April of 1995 you moved to the southern post. What were you doing there? What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What were you doing there in March, April of 1995 in this southern post or facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did the same type of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why we're -- he's been telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Court is satisfied, that's fine. I will not argue with the Court about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think there's no point in starting with the next cross-examination now. We'll have the break. Let's revise a little bit, because of course we have other things to do as well. First of all, I just wanted to confirm to you that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Judge Stole will -- something urgent cropped up for him and he will probably be able to join us during the next session, but he couldn't make it for this first session. That's what I wanted to say. The other thing is this: Do you still require 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that even 15 minutes will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Lazarevic -- sorry, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We decided not to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. She -- yes, they didn't translate it into English. She probably will not have any questions, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Josse, I don't know. You had intimated nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Our position remains the same, the Court will be glad to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Sarapa or Mr. Haynes? You said possibly 10 minutes, possibly, but also possibly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most likely nothing, and if there is anything, five minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But still, I was for a moment thinking of whether we could go on but I think it would be wiser to have the break, because the 15, 10 minutes could suddenly become 20 and I wouldn't like to leave the staff here. All right. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Half an hour, yes, because we need to discuss some outstanding motions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Stole should be with us soon, if we are still here. Yes. Mr. Zivanovic will go next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you explained to us that, amongst other things, sometimes you also typed these reports into the computer. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please clarify one thing to which you already replied to but it wasn't quite clear to me. In the heading of the report were you able to type in the date and number or was this something that was assigned automatically by the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would get the heading as soon as we opened a new document for typing. There was the macro at the top where there was a place for the date. I don't know whether this was entered automatically. You had to put the time in by hand and also the participants. I cannot remember about the date, whether it was done automatically on the basis of the computer date or whether you had to type in it by hand. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you cannot remember about the number of the reports either. Was this generated automatically by the computer or did you have to type it in yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you -- your assumption is all right. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were shown an intercept between Krstic and Obrenovic which you noted in the notebook on the 2nd of August, 1995. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I have it under Wednesday here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And you also saw the typed version of that intercept. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you yourself typed that intercept into the computer? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were any problems in sending off that intercept or that report to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you clarify what kind of problems you are thinking of? You can have different kinds of problem. So if you can just maybe clarify that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be much better to show you a document; that is Defence Exhibit 1D93. Can you please look at this document and then tell me if this perhaps jogs your memory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. This document that I'm looking at now is something that I never saw in my life when I was in Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you don't remember any such problem cropping up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that our computer technician would know. We didn't really discuss this sort of thing much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you also mentioned some technical problems or some technical aspects that affect the sound quality when the intercepts are being found.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the distance from the antenna affect the quality of reception?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, distance does have an effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, if you know, in view of your technical qualifications in respect of these matters what this distance would be enabling intercepts to be monitored from an RRU1 device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the technical data, but I can tell you something else. For example, if the elevation that is picking up those waves, that would be 230 to 270 megahertz, and particularly if the antennas that are being listened to are visible from our elevation, then the reception is very good. If you look at ham operators, we can have very good antenna contacts at much higher frequencies, and that is more difficult. But here it was much easier in our case to do it because that is the kind of wavelength that it was possible to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how far your elevation was from the axis that was being monitored?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't tell you, but I could very easily calculate that on the map if you showed it to me and if that's what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how far your facility, the southern facility, where you were, is from the northern facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that it was just perhaps a couple of kilometres as the crow flies, but I cannot give you a precise number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximate distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could give you an approximate distance. As the crow flies, it could be from 15 to 20 kilometres, up to 22 kilometres distance as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question. Does that mean that the distance is not important if you have optical visibility, if you have visual objectives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important, but not to such a degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Madam Nikolic, I understand no questions. Mr. Lazarevic, no questions. I just -- I know, but I'm just reconfirming, that's all. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very few questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the typist, the one typing the conversation, was the typist given only that task of typing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the task of that person, the only one, but that person was also capable of working. So sometimes if we couldn't press a button and stop and he was close by, he would be able to do something like that. But he mostly carried out the typing assignments. He was trained for other kind of work, but that was his main assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the person would themselves intercept the conversation, would they also be in charge of intercepting conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever was in the shift would stop the device when a signal was picked up, and they would try to record it on the tape. That was our job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that you have understood the question. The question is with reference to the typist, would the typist also during the shift have the responsibility of logging in and intercepting conversations, or would his or her work be restricted only to typing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. The person entrusted with the typing would only do the typing. That was his main task. Intercepting conversations is something I -- I really never saw anything like that happen when I was on my shift intercepting conversations. I never saw anything like that happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, the person in charge of typing the conversations, was that person subordinated to the same commander as you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I suppose, or Mr. Josse, I'm confirming that they have no questions. I'm going through this for the record more than anything. Yes, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So no questions. Is there re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Sir, my learned friend Mr. Ostojic asked or suggested to you that the first time you spoke about whether Colonel Beara was known or unknown to you at the time you took down the intercepted conversation was during a recent proofing. Do you recall, sir, whether or not you testified about that topic in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I read a portion of your testimony would that refresh your recollection about whether or not you testified about that topic in the Krstic case, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
