utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Thayer. I mean, it's almost a rhetorical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, just for the record, we're looking at the transcript in Krstic on page 4472, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, what my colleague is doing now is trying to use something that is not on the record. So he's using a past statement. There's a procedure for this. So one, I an appreciate the question that he did put to the witness, but now we can just take the page and show it to the witness. It does not have to be read into the transcript. The witness can look at it and say whether that does refresh his memory and then answer the question that my colleague asked, but not to read part of that transcript in -- of the Krstic transcript into these proceedings. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to read it too. I mean, we have to know what it says. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, with all due respect, it wasn't a question of whether he says he's known to him. It was the question of the voice that we suggested to him, and the point was that he recollected or recalled that he knew his voice at that time. And clearly we know what it says on Krstic, because we invited him to bring in that evidence and whether he said that in whatever manner he did. So the question has nothing to do what I was asking about. So I think it's beyond -- he's asked him if he knew him, if he claims he knew him. I asked him specifically about his recollection which was added on the 11th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It makes it even more obvious that we need to see what he allegedly said in Krstic, because otherwise how can we establish whether this is a proper re-examination? Exactly. So let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. So please proceed with reading out to the witness the excerpt from Krstic. I am making it clear on behalf of the Trial Chamber to you that that part that you are reading is not being introduced as evidence in this case. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that is, I hope, properly understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The question is: "Q. This type of conversation that we have just referred to in Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit 328, was this conversation classified as an important one? "A. This conversation was taped because a colonel, Ljubo Beara, and General Krstic appear. They were very well-known figures at the time." Sir, does that refresh your recollection as to whether you testified about that topic as to whether Colonel Beara was known or unknown to you at the time you took this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it doesn't -- if it doesn't follow yours, it follows Judge Kwon's.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I would just say mischaracterises what it says, but enough said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can -- you can make submissions. Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Both microphones for the witness are turned off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both microphones for the witness are turned off. While mine is on when it should be off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? At the time, Colonel Beara's was known to me. I recognised it because I would listen to him from the tape a lot of times and also from other conversations, unimportant ones, meaning that I did recognise the voice at the time for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think you've missed the point, Witness. I don't think the point was to seek again a repetition from you that you recognised the voice because you were familiar with it at the time. I think the light of -- the substance of Mr. Thayer's point in reading out what you allegedly said in Krstic is to point out to you that on that occasion, according to him and according to the transcript, you didn't just mention that you recognised the voice, but you also said that this -- who you describe as Colonel Beara and Krstic were very well-known persons to you at the time. This is the point that I suppose Mr. Thayer is addressing you to. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I just wanted to clarify. I'm not making the point that in Krstic this witness testified concerning voice recognition. That was not the case, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I just didn't want anyone to think that I was trying to get more than is what is in the transcript, that is all. Shall we put the question again or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please. He is not my witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just didn't know whether there was another clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just brought him forward because he missed your point, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were not on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will try to adjust the frequency, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he will recognise the modulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, having had that portion of the prior testimony read to you, does that refresh your recollection in any way concerning whether or not at the time you took down that conversation Colonel Beara was known or unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for clarification of the record, so we can settle this. I see in the transcript the word is "it was known to me." Was Colonel Beara known to you at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time he was known to me. I had heard of him several times, from other friends of mine even from the command when we would exchange visits. He was known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to follow up on a question His Honour Judge Kwon asked you, sir. As you sit here today, do you recall whether at the time you took this conversation down you knew anything more about Colonel Beara other than he was a colonel and his name, as reflected in the intercept transcription you wrote down, for example, unit, or any other information, as you sit here today can you recall whether you had more knowledge about him then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That concludes my redirect. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One point that clarifies that. It just disappeared. Give me a minute. Yes. It's at page 48, line 18. The witness to the question to Mr. Thayer answered: "At that time, Colonel Beara's," probably voice, "was known to me. I recognised it because I would listen to him from the tape a lot of times, and also from other conversations." What tape do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tape that we had recorded then at that time, and because of the bad quality, then we would have to listen to it over and over, if something was missing, if we didn't transcribe a word properly. And that is why I recalled the modulation, regardless of whether I wanted to or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you had heard something not important, unimportant conversation, you would have erased it without having to rehear it through the tape? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If there was nothing important or if there was a new frequency, that would be new information for us. Or if there was a new name, we would note that down. But if there was nothing new, if it was all old information or if the conversation itself was unimportant, we would re-record over the tape. We would go back to zero or wherever we started from, and then we would record a new conversation over that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you are saying that you heard the tape a lot of times, then, you referred to the specific tape of this conversation, be it 15th or 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-133 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no further questions for you, sir, which means your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Tribunal, I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony. Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom and the rest of the staff assists you upon your return become home, and on behalf of everyone here, I would like to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm informed Mr. Bourgon would like to say something. Or, rather, let's go the exhibits first. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We've tendered the exhibit list. I can enumerate them or we can proceed as we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Has the list been circulated?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes it has, Your Honour. I think everybody has a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with the usual caveat on the admissibility of intercepts? Do you have any objection to the introduction into evidence of any of these documents? I hear none. Those in bold print -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object to Exhibit 1385 because this is the intercept that was not mentioned by this witness in the Blagojevic case, nor was it mentioned in the past two days in this trial. Therefore, it wasn't showed to this witness except in proofing for the evidence when he met with the OTP as he was preparing to testify in our trial. In addition to that, in the pre-trial brief for Witness 76 in relation to the summary done for this witness, this intercept is not mentioned at all as one of the items that he will be asked about and that he will be giving evidence before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What would you like to say about this, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, briefly. The item has been on this witness's exhibit list for some time. The Defence has been aware of this exhibit. It has been provided to them in hard copy and other forms with 65 ter numbers and the packet. It is the -- our position that the foundation has been laid for these exhibits which we are choosing not to show the individual witness during the testimony. He testified that he reviewed the packet. He identified his handwriting, his handwritten notebooks, or his handwritten transcription, that he compared that with the actual notebooks, that the copies in the packet were fair and accurate, that if they were a transcription that he identified that as well. And we believe the foundation has been laid. That is the procedure we have been following so that we don't need to show every single witness every single intercept. We will have, in addition, further testimony from Ms. Frease that will ultimately tie --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Do you wish to add anything, or is it finished, your submission is over?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My submission is over, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the position is the following: That we do want a confirmation from you that when you referred the witness to the packet yesterday in the beginning of your examination-in-chief, this 1385, particularly the one which is a photocopy of the handwritten notebook, was included in the packet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, it's not a question that I had doubt in my mind, but we have also a record to look after. So that is a confirmation. Our position is that then the Prosecution doesn't have to put to the witness each and every document that it is relying to specifically. I mean, this was put to the witness as a document contained in the package that he was asked questions upon, and therefore the objection to the admission of 1385 as based -- or as expounded by Ms. Nikolic is not being entertained. Of course, there is the issue, other issues relating to intercepts in general, so these documents, the intercepts and the handwritten notebook, will be marked for identification purposes. The transcript of the testimony in Blagojevic will become P02333, and it will remain under seal for obvious reasons, and so will the pseudonym sheet. Now, Mr. Ostojic, would you like to tender any document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only document will be identified as 1D70, 7-0. So 1D70, which is the information report on November 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's Ms. Frease's information, report, if I understand you well, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection. I just request that it be placed under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And so it is so admitted under seal. No further documents, I suppose. Okay. So that closes that chapter. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, four submissions to make. I'll try to move as quickly as I can in order not to waste too much time. The first submission, Mr. President, deals with a decision issued by the Deputy Registrar on the 29th of November of this year concerning the partly indigent status of our client, Mr. Nikolic. We believe that the Deputy Registrar misdirected himself in law in that decision, and we intend to ask for a review before the Trial Chamber in accordance with the directive on the assignment of Defence counsel. Pursuant to that directive, we have 15 days to make such a request for review. The deadline would therefore be today, on the 14th of December. We are not in a position to make our request for review today because we have not been able to meet with the duty counsel who was assigned to represent Mr. Nikolic at the time when he appeared before the Tribunal for the first time and at the time when he filled in what we call the declaration of means. So accordingly, we respectfully request an extension of time in accordance with Rule 126 to file our request until we've had and opportunity to meet with the duty counsel. We know who he is, and we have -- we did try to approach him, and that could be until Friday the 22nd of December, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's point one. Let's move to matter number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The second issue is the -- the second submission deals with the -- and I need to go into private session for this one, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The next submission, Mr. President, deals with Prosecution motion for order of protection for the new Witness P108. Mr. President, we will respond to this motion in writing, of course, in accordance with the Rules. However, this motion places us in a difficult situation which needs to be addressed at this time. There is a witness out there called P108, and all we know that he lives -- he or she lives in Zvornik. We don't know what -- what he will testify about, and we don't know his identity. All we know is that according to the Prosecution this would be, of course, bad evidence, as if the Prosecution could bring exculpatory witness -- an exculpatory witness but that's not really the issue. This causes us two practical difficulties. First, is we've been meeting with lots of people in Zvornik, and we continue to meet with people in the Zvornik area, and we will do so during the winter recess, and this place us in the potential difficult situation concerning that maybe we've met this person already and we don't know, or possibly that we could run into this person over the winter recess. Secondly, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision on the Rule 65 motion, on the Prosecution motion to amend the Rule 65 list, this witness could be called as early as 15 January, which makes it very difficult for us to plan the way ahead in terms of preparations of the case for the Defence. We believe it is inappropriate for the name of this witness, or at least part of the contents, the subject matter of his testimony, to be concealed from us, and we take the view that this creates actually more risk than less to the security of this witness. If the security threat is so high as the Prosecution says it is, then there might be another less severe way to handle this, and maybe one thing that could be looked upon is disclosure of subject matter for counsel eyes only. But at least something that will allow us to know what this Witness P108 is about. And that's the third submission, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a fourth and final submission which deals with the Rule 65 ter summary which was provided by the Prosecution for the witness that we -- that has just completed his testimony. Now that is that the testimony of this witness is over, we are in a position to compare what he said and what he testified about with what was announced in the summary. Now, we argued that at the beginning of this case that the summaries prepared by the Prosecution did not reflect the Prosecution's case and they should be treated with the greatest care. This one is a very good example. Pursuant to this summary, the witness was to testify about a conversation which took place on the 2nd of August between General Krstic and Major -- it says Major Obrenovic, where Krstic ordered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Bourgon, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I'm terribly sorry to interrupt you, but I just want to clarify when you're speaking about a summary, are you speaking about a summary that was read out to us in court or are you speaking about the summary that's on the 65 ter documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge. I was looking at my notes. I'm talking about Rule 65 ter summary that was joined to the pre-trial brief, not the summary that was provided by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify that. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I just quote this -- this was Witness 76 in the summary, and the summary read as follows: "The conversation between General Krstic and Major Obrenovic where Krstic orders Obrenovic to kill all the prisoners Obrenovic had captured." Now, when we look at -- when we know that this conversation took place on the 2nd of August but we've had the testimony, and what we know now is that this did not deal with prisoners and this did not deal with persons that had been captured, yet that was in the summary. And to us there are many examples like this where either the contents of the summary does not reflect the Prosecution's case or where the Prosecution is leading evidence that goes beyond what was announced in the summaries. For this, Mr. President, we think that this is a source of the delays that we have sometimes in this trial, and the object of our submissions today is that at the beginning of the case the Defence has highlighted difficulties with the Prosecution pre-trial brief. We said that there were defects, and we asked the Trial Chamber to respectfully look into the situation and maybe order the Prosecution to file a new brief. The pre-trial brief is a document that we use throughout the case, especially in this case when we're trying to find -- find out where the Prosecution is going with this case, and given that this is a document that still contains defects, we would like the Trial Chamber, Mr. President, respectfully to look into this situation and order the Prosecution to cure those defects. Thank you, Mr. President. That was my fourth and final submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Bourgon, before you sit down, in the beginning of the sitting I referred you to also protective measures sought for Witness number 80; in other words, the Prosecution's request to have remaining in place the measures already implemented in the Krstic trial vis-a-vis this witness. Do you have a common position so that we can rule on it orally now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I believe we have already stated our position that there was no objection to the measures requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my impression, but I just wanted a confirmation of it. All right. I seem to have it. So we can start with that. Judge Prost and Judge Kwon? So we confirm first and foremost - and this is an oral decision - the orders put in place, the protective measures put in place in regard to Witness number 80. Now, Mr. McCloskey, I don't think it's the case of dealing with the first point raised by Mr. Bourgon relating to the pretended indigence of his client as established by the registrar in his decision, or do you wish to address it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, no problem. That's not our -- our place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move to the -- it doesn't mean that I will not come back to you, Mr. Bourgon, on this. Second issue, protective measures motion relating to the proposed December witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I don't have a -- I don't have a problem with additional time with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't have a problem with that. Number three, the issue relating to P108. We are aware, as you are, that on -- I don't remember the date, but we -- in relation to this witness, we had given the Prosecution two options, either to immediately disclose the identity of PW-0108 to the Defence or submit a submission for protective measures no later than the 12th of December, which obviously you opted for the second option that we had indicated and we are dealing with that. There is an objection on the part of Mr. Bourgon that this still puts them in the precarious situation of not knowing the name of this individual and the inability therefore when they visit Zvornik in the proximate few weeks to try to gather information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. I think this is a matter to be dealt with in the filings. It's a very serious matter, and we have made our filing. I -- this witness is in a very dangerous situation. There have been people in this situation murdered, and -- and I just think this is serious enough that -- an off-the-cuff kind of surprise motion. I mean, we will -- we'll look at the record, and if we need to respond in more detail we will, but I think this is something that is proper for the filings. I disagree with him, and I -- and we're not in a position at this point to -- I mean, we'll always talk with Mr. Bourgon, and if there's a way to work it out, we will. On a practical -- we can see that we want to bunch those intercept operators, so we're not going to be getting to this witness for a while, and so in -- so it's not really a -- a crucial issue right now, but I'll try to work anything out. But I -- this is a serious enough issue I really would like to stick with our submissions and go over them before I say something that I don't recall or I get mixed up about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There was also a suggestion by Mr. Bourgon that perhaps a way out would be disclosure of this person's identity to the Defence counsel, Defence counsel only. Do you wish to address that now, or do you wish to give it thought?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's problematic, Your Honour, not because I think anyone's doing anything they shouldn't be, but once they have that information, they will ask questions about it. The word gets out. Zvornik is right now a place where there's a lot of tension and lot of concern by -- on the witnesses that are there, and part of that is because people are -- are there asking questions and mentioning names. So that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position as it seems, and we wouldn't be saying much, obviously, is that on the face of it at the present moment the Prosecution's motion seeking protective measures, the protective measures indicated in that motion for this witness, P108, is in compliance with our previous decision. So that's -- that's the starting point. So if you think that that aggravates your position in any way, we are not going to suggest anything that -- to you. I mean, it's up to you to decide how best to protect your client's interests, and we will then deal with the matter as and when we are seized with it. Yes, and then there was the last issue raised by Mr. Bourgon, and that is a complaint relating to the 65 ter summaries to wit and in particular this persons, this last witness's 65 ter summaries, and possible suggestion that maybe it's the case of calling on you to re-propose a fresh pre-trial brief with updated and more correct information contained in the summaries. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm looking at our summary, and in my view it is -- it's accurate. It is concise, and it gave a pretty good explanation and outline of what this person will testify to. That and the fact that I believe it was a 92 ter witness where we're -- where we're referring the -- where we're referring the Defence to testimony there can be no surprise about where he's coming from. Now, on the particular point Mr. Bourgon is mentioning, that -- something about that this is -- that Obrenovic is not talking about prisoners and that we have misstated it. The -- if you go to that intercept, you'll see that Krstic says something to the effect, "How's it go?" Obrenovic says, "Ah, we've got some more on minefields and at gunpoint." And Mr. Obrenovic was referring to Muslims, prisoners that they've taken. And if you take a look at the daily combat report for August 2nd, you will see that same situation talked about. And so when General Krstic says three times to kill them all, it is our view that what he's referring to are those people that they've captured at gunpoint during August 2nd. And as you've seen evidence and you'll see further evidence of people going through the woods and getting killed, this is what this is talking about. It's right on point. It's in the Krstic -- probably the Krstic judgement -- or excuse me, the Krstic testimony which went through this intercept at length. He got his facts completely wrong, and luckily I'm here and I lived that and so I can respond on my feet. But when there are going to be serious allegations like this to what is a serious document, the 65 ter list, we have no problem with a brief mentioning of it and then a filing so we can accurately respond. But when these kind of frivolous comments are going to be made on important documents where a simple reading of the facts would -- would make it clear, that's a problem. Luckily I'm here, I'm healthy and I can respond to it, but it's really a problem. But it's Christmas, and Mr. Ostojic had invited me to talk about that a bit more, and I can if -- if we'd like. There's other witnesses, Dr. French, other things like that, but that's -- that would be my response to Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Bourgon, very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President. That might be the Prosecution's theory of the case. That's very different from what a witness is going to be called to say, and this witness has never mentioned anything about prisoners. And my reading of that intercept, there is absolutely nothing about. It's more of a fighting situation and nothing about prisoners. So it's what the witness will talk about. And these witness summaries have to be treated with great care. But the object of my intervention at this time was to call upon the Trial Chamber to look at what we said about the pre-trial brief at the beginning of the case. Those problems still exist and do not allow us to work with the pre-trial brief, and we kindly ask, Mr. President, respectfully that you look into the pre-trial brief to see. Because at the beginning, if you recall, you mentioned that this could be a problem also for Your Honours and your staff working on this case, and I simply ask that you look at this document and you see whether these comments that we made at the beginning are still there and, if so, to intervene and order the Prosecution to cure the defects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we've heard enough on this, Mr. McCloskey. We are not going to ask you to revise your pre-trial brief taking into consideration what the proposed witnesses of the Defence will be saying. So we can leave it at that. Now, give us one minute to decide on the extension issues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, do you view a 65 ter -- the summary or pre-trial brief as kind of evidence? I have difficulty following your objection. Prosecution is entitled to put their case into their brief and summary, as they understand it, but we never take it as a part of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Our submission -- our submission, Your Honour, is that these of course 65 ter summary, they are not evidence nor should they be treated as evidence. However, it is our view that those summaries are a tool which can be used by Your Honours as well as by the staff within Chambers in order to prepare for the hearing of a witness. And if these summaries reflect information that is different from the real -- from the case that will be led when the witness appears, then it is something that can influence the process. That's what we're saying. It's not helpful to have a summary that goes beyond what the witness will talk about. And in the same regard, it doesn't help if that summary says something and then the witness comes and says more. There are decisions in -- before other Trial Chambers where as soon as the witness goes beyond the 65 ter summary then the witness is stopped and the Prosecution cannot lead further evidence. That's all we're saying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you we'll never see that happening in this Trial Chamber. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would invite Mr. Bourgon and all other Defence counsel if there's a particular summary they think is lacking and they want more information, come to us. It's the first time I've heard this. And this summary was right on the money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So there are two requests that you have made, Mr. Bourgon. The first one for an extended period for the filing of your response or position or motion, and one relating to the registrar's decision on the partial indigence and also corresponding -- of costs relating to your client. You're seeking an extension up to the 22nd of December. We are granting you that extension. You also seek an extension up to the same date in order to be able to consider more fully the new points raised in the follow-up to the Prosecution motion for protective measures for the December witnesses. You're seeking an additional period up to the 22nd of December. We are also granting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President. The second request was not for additional time. It was to file an additional response, because there has been already motion, response, and reply, and now we just want to have an opportunity to respond to issues that were raised in the reply that we could not respond before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the permission to file the additional response. Which brings me to perhaps the most enjoyable part of today's sitting. Please allow me on behalf of -- yes. I hear that Mr. Ostojic has some submissions to make in the absence of Mr. Thayer. Or Mr. Thayer is still here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He gets my e-mails actually often but never replies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In any event, Your Honour, there's two points, one that was raised by my learned friend Mr. McCloskey a couple of weeks ago regarding the aerial images and the testimony of Mr. Ruez. I just want to be clear because I think it was just said in a time when we weren't discussing it. I want just our position to be clear. We don't want Mr. Ruez back. We want to interrogate him further on the aerial images. We did get the response from the embassy of the United States of America which I think confirms that the questions we asked were appropriate. The only question I'd like to ask the Court is to help us get the letter from the OTP that they sent to the embassy dated the 21st of October this year where they outlined the areas. What we are specifically concerned with is, if the Court will recall, the images and how they're, in our view at least with all due respect, somewhat inconsistent. There's an emblem on one but not on all, there's dates on some, and I'm just summarising it for the Court, and I think I'm accurate. So we want our position to be clear. We would like it in this break if you could schedule. I know Mr. Ruez might be on his island or wherever he goes in the winter, but we'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think and again we are -- I wasn't expecting this, so whatever I say is subject to control and agreement with my two colleagues. But our understanding to my knowledge is that there has been an exchange of correspondence between Mr. McCloskey and the Defence teams, and the last we heard of was a sort of an invitation from Mr. McCloskey to you to come forward with what exactly you wish to convey by way of information for the US embassy to be able to determine exactly the outcome of the request by -- by Mr. McCloskey. So to our knowledge we are waiting for the feedback from Mr. McCloskey based, I would suppose, on the follow-up, but we haven't heard anything. So I don't know what has been happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to point that out and we'll clarify that over the break and get that to the Court. The second issue I have, and this would be the last issue, Your Honour, is we've been dealing with the registry with respect to our learned friend Mr. Nebojsa Mrkic here is our now -- technically our assistant. The registrar as recently as yesterday, the 13th, has referred us to the Court to make a decision. We have applied that Mr. Mrkic, who previously has been a judge in the former Yugoslavia for eight and a half years, is an experienced lawyer, that he have an audience with this Court on a very limited basis. And what we're suggesting is because of the workload and the witnesses that might or are expected to be somewhat sped up in light of the fact also that the Prosecution has, I think, five or six different Prosecutors assisting in the presentation of evidence, we would request respectfully from this Court that you grant Mr. Mrkic the opportunity to cross-examine five to seven witnesses during the OTP case, and seven to 10 during our Defence case so that we can more efficiently go through the evidence and make a presentation to the Court. The registry, and I think I gave the letter to -- they've sent a response saying to defer it to the Court. He at all times will be under our supervision. We will be present, either Mr. Meek or myself, during those times, and we're requesting that orally now so that we could proceed in the next session and organise which witnesses, if the Court allows, he may examine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But of course we are taken - I speak for myself - completely by surprise on this. What I suggest is that following -- as a follow-up to this letter to you by Mr. Martin Petrov dated 13 December, you follow up with a proper formal request, and I suggest that it would be extremely, extremely helpful that we are at least put in the same position that enabled Mr. Petrov to reach this conclusion. In other words, that we have a proper indication of Mr. Mrkic's background, his CV, experience and whatever. I think that is fundamental to whatever motion. If this materialises, when would be -- do you already have in mind the specific witnesses that -- Prosecution witnesses that he will cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not with all seven but we do have specifically three witnesses that we have been discussing and would like, in accordance with our client's wishes also, to have Mr. Mrkic cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And would these be amongst the January testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I haven't yet received the January witness list but they might be. But two other points for your consideration I must put on the record. One, my learned Mr. McCloskey, we've talked about it well over a month ago, he has no objection to it whatsoever, and I gave him the same parameters as I've shared with the Court. And also the ADC has said that they have no objection to us seeking this and of approving Mr. Mrkic as acting in the limited basis as another co-counsel in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think -- yes, Mr. McCloskey. Do you want to put on record?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. While we will certainly miss Mr. Ostojic's cross-examination, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, do you associate yourself? Yes, I think we can leave it at that. We will give this --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will give this all due consideration, and we will be awaiting your formal request. I think it has to be followed up by a formal request --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and attendant documents. Which brings me to what I had in mind to say before we break -- we break for this festive season. We have basically been living together, this trial, for a number of months now, intensively I would say, but also positively and profitably. I think we all agree on that. We are now all looking forward to a well-merited, well-deserved short break, relatively speaking, over which some of us will be celebrating Christmas, I don't know if all, and also some other religious feasts. We will all certainly be celebrating the arrival of the new year, if not the end of the present one, and so on behalf of Judge Kwon, Judge Prost, on behalf also of Judge Stole, who because of very serious reasons couldn't be with us this morning, I wish to extend to you and to your families and loved ones our warmest and most heart-felt greetings and best wishes for this festive season and also for the entire new year that hopefully will see us back all together on January the 10th when we start again. Thank you.
